Issued at 115 AM EST Sun Nov 15 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Cutoff low over Newfoundland and associated longwave troughing to 
ease its grip on the region the next couple days as ridging over the 
plains and associated surface high pressure centered over Wisconsin 
moves into the region. Ongoing cyclonic flow regime continues to 
generate some lake induced instability with the 00z APX RAOB 
showcasing a stubborn low-level saturation layer beneath an 
inversion at 850mb. With meager low level lapse rates and a lack of 
saturation reaching into the DGZ, this activity is drizzle at this 
point. Already seeing evidence of height rises from Plains ridging 
within the aforementioned RAOB, with drier air aloft building. As 
subsidence intrudes with the arrival of the surface high to the 
south, the cessation of lake effect activity is anticipated 
throughout the day as warmer air aloft stymies lake induced 
instability plumes. As the surface high moves into southern Ontario 
/ northern Ohio by Monday, ample return flow to build in conjunction 
with a developing system over the Canadian Prairies reinvigorating a 
pinched pressure gradient. Result will be the return of well-above 
normal temperatures and drier conditions through the week amid 
occasionally breezy conditions. Weak wave to ride this area of 
quicker flow Thursday before a potentially larger system builds in 
some time next weekend.

Details: 

Noticing a sharp downward trend with ongoing lake induced drizzle 
across NW lower into north-central lower. Evidence of the incoming 
high pressure and subsidence aloft already showing its hand. As 
such, anticipating any lingering drizzle to conclude later tonight, 
with just some stubborn low-level cloud to hang around through the 
morning, especially across NW lower where lake influences will hold 
strongest. Regardless, anticipating a slow clearing trend to 
materialize this afternoon, which will offer a setup conducive for 
efficient radiational cooling late tonight into Monday morning. With 
several days of damp weather under our belt, anticipation is that 
decoupling winds from the weaker pressure gradient courtesy of the 
surface high moving over lower MI will allow for fog to develop late 
tonight into Monday. How early this fog develops will be dependent 
on how quick clouds clear this afternoon (earlier break in clouds, 
later fog development, and vice versa). Once we get into Monday, the 
surface high will have more or less parked itself in the vicinity of 
Lake Erie and Ohio for the next several days. Warmer SWerly flow to 
prevail through the week, drawing in a markedly warmer airmass... 
with temperatures in the 50s and possibly even 60s in downsloping 
locales by Tuesday Keep in mind, average highs are generally between 
39 and 45 degrees this time of year. Overall, the forecast looks dry 
this week, aside from a wave passing through the upper Great Lakes 
some time between Thursday and Thursday night. 

Lack of agreement on guidance brings uncertainty on rainfall 
amounts, coverage, and duration for this system. Nonetheless, 
guidance is on board with a system passing through. Another wave to 
eject into the Plains after midweek, with most guidance members 
depicting an aggressively deepening surface low over Minnesota. 
Given pattern recognition and amplification biases in long-term 
guidance, this system will probably occlude itself into oblivion 
before it reaches here, which will probably lead to a return of 
widespread, lighter precipitation (mainly rain, at least to start) 
at some point through the weekend, with a colder push on the 
backside of the system eventually leading to a returning chance for 
light snow. No glaring signals for a massive lake effect outburst, 
as the occluded nature of the system probably stymies the overlap of 
best low-level synoptic moisture and a colder low-level airmass to 
drum up those lake effect snow bands. Nonetheless, colder weather 
set to return either by the conclusion of the upcoming weekend or by 
early next week. More details to come.
